page.lead: Every database below is compared on the same columns, read from its own documentation, licence file, release notes and, where they exist, independent Jepsen tests. All cells were checked on 4 October 2026. The starting point is the one the Reading tab argues for: PostgreSQL is the default, and every other row is read as an escape hatch you take when a measured problem forces you off it, which is why each row ends with "why leave Postgres for it".
page.howto:
How to use this
Answer the five questions to mark candidate rows, or filter by family, storage engine, licence and how it runs. Switch the column set to see one aspect at a time (on a phone, swipe the table sideways). Click a row for every field with numbered sources; tick "+" on up to three rows to compare them. Words like B-tree, LSM-tree or snapshot isolation are explained in the box below and taught properly in the Reading tab.
page.foot: Data: src/atlas/research (one file per system), merged by src/atlas/build_atlas.py with overrides.json and chooser.json; claims in src/atlas/claims.json. Version numbers come from each project's release page or GitHub releases on 4 October 2026; managed services have no version, so their row shows the date of a recent dated change instead. Vendor performance and cost figures are labelled as vendor claims; Jepsen reports are independent tests of one version at one date and say nothing about later versions unless retested.

permissive.tip: OSI licence such as Apache 2.0, MIT, BSD, PostgreSQL: use, change and sell freely

glossary.d: Several changes that all happen or none do. "Multi-row" means the all-or-nothing covers many rows; many stores only promise it for one item or one document.

How much two transactions running at the same time can see of each other. From weakest: read committed (you never see uncommitted data), snapshot isolation or repeatable read (you read one frozen moment), serializable (the result is as if transactions ran one at a time).

A commit is durable when it survives a power cut. That needs the write flushed to the disk (fsync) before the database says "done"; some stores acknowledge first and flush later, so the last moments can be lost.
A replica is a copy kept up to date from the primary. If copying is asynchronous, reading a replica can return slightly old data, and a crash of the primary can lose writes it had acknowledged.
Splitting the data across servers by a key (for example user id), so each server holds a part. The shard or partition key is hard to change later because every row would move.
Ways for a group of servers to agree on each write, so that a majority must confirm it. They give consistency across servers at the cost of a network round trip per write.
"Enough replicas answered": with 3 copies, writing to 2 and reading from 2 guarantees the read sees the write. Leaderless stores such as Cassandra let you choose per query.
A sorted tree of fixed-size pages, updated in place. Finding one row takes a few page reads, which is why it is the default index for transactional databases.
Log-structured merge tree: writes go to memory, are flushed to disk as sorted files and merged (compacted) in the background. Very fast writes; reads may check several files.
Each column of a table stored together and compressed. A query that adds up one column reads only that column; changing one row means touching many blocks.
Multi-version concurrency control: the database keeps old versions of a row so readers see a consistent snapshot while writers make new versions, and readers do not block writers.
Approximate nearest neighbour search finds vectors close to a query without checking all of them, trading a little recall for speed. HNSW is the common index: a layered graph walked greedily.
For text search: a map from each word to the documents containing it. BM25 is the standard score: rarer words count more, and repeating a word helps less each time.

An independent tester (Kyle Kingsbury) who breaks clusters on purpose (network cuts, crashes, clock jumps) and checks whether a database keeps the guarantees its documentation claims, for one version at one date.

The code is readable and usable, but offering the product as a competing managed service is forbidden or restricted; the Open Source Initiative does not count them as open source. BSL code turns open source after a set number of years.
The database is a library running inside your program, reading files directly: no server, no network hop, one machine.

questions.q: What will you mostly ask of the data?
questions.h: Start from the queries, not the shape of the data: nearly any shape fits nearly any store, but each store is fast at some questions only.

opts.t: Scan and add up millions of rows

questions.q: Must several rows change together, all or nothing?
questions.h: Example: debiting a balance and inserting the usage record. If yes, you want real multi-row transactions inside one store.

questions.q: How many writes per second at the peak?
questions.h: The peak and the hottest key decide this, not the average.

opts.t: Hundreds of thousands, or several regions

questions.q: Do you know every query you will need?
questions.h: Unknown future questions favour SQL over normalised tables; fixed, known access paths are what license a specialised store.

opts.t: No, the product is still changing
Yes, the access paths are fixed

questions.q: What can your team operate at 3 a.m.?
questions.h: Count backups, tested restores, failover, upgrades and who gets paged.

wr.1: comfortable up to a few thousand writes per second on one primary
wr.2: handles tens of thousands of writes per second
wr.3: designed to scale writes out across many servers or regions

wrshort.1: a few thousand writes per second
wrshort.2: tens of thousands of writes per second

ops.server: runs as a single server you can operate
ops.lib: runs as a library in your process
